extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / natural philosophers, instrument-makers, physicians and astronomers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical methods and performance criteria for constructing and using scientific instruments (microscopes, speaking trumpets), observational procedures for eclipses and astronomy, mechanical-engine performance measures, and standards for anatomical post-mortem reporting as presented in a Philosophical Transactions issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscope lens (bead) making
rubrics_metrics.description: Best method to make very small clear glass lenses (size of a large pin's head and smaller). "The best way of all I have yet found, to make them clear and without specks, is with the flame of spirit of wine well rectified, and burned in a lamp."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise procedure and workmanship tolerances: use a lamp burning rectified spirit of wine (rather than tallow- or wax-flame); use very small silver wire doubled like a skein (wet with spirit) to give an ardent flame; take beaten glass washed very clean on the point of a silver needle filed very small and wet with spittle; hold in the flame till quite round but not longer ("for fear of burning it"); if the side next the needle be not melted, remove and take it up on the round side and present the rough side to the flame till everywhere very round and smooth; then wipe and rub one or several of them together with soft leather to improve them; mount between two thin brass pieces with very round apertures (the eye-side aperture almost as large as the glass diameter) and place in a frame with the object conveniently for observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscope mounting / aperture sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: How to mount small spherical lenses into a usable microscope assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After forming and polishing the glass bead, put them between two pieces of thin brass whose apertures are very round, with the aperture towards the eye almost as large as the diameter of the glass; place the assembly in a frame with the object positioned conveniently for observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eclipse observation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical method for observing solar eclipses and recording accurate times and appearances. "The image of the sun, through the telescope, was received on a whiter paper, and the appearances carefully noted. The times were corrected by the altitudes of the sun, taken by the shadow of a gnomon erected for the purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project the telescope image onto a white screen/paper and carefully note visual appearances (horn positions, vertical/horizontal orientation). Correct timing by using solar altitude measurements derived from a gnomon's shadow to adjust recorded times. Record principal phases with precise timestamps and note geometric relations (e.g. horns vertical/horizontal) to deduce relative diameters and positions of lunar/solar centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and testing criteria for reflecting speaking trumpets
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric/material design and empirical performance expectations for a reflecting speaking trumpet. Described trumpet: a large concave pyramid (about a yard long) with a concave head and an internal bended tube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction notes and performance tests: the instrument may be built of wood, tin (tinned iron plate), pewter, stone, bell-metal, etc.; the inner bended tube and concave receiver concentrate sound. Empirical test reported: distinct delivery of certain words across a garden and the Thames, even against strong wind, and words were written down by a receiver. Advantages: may send voice as far as long trumpets while reducing near-field noise and enabling indoor use. Also note failed variants: angular arches can shorten delivery or obstruct sound (one-arch shortens, three-arch almost wholly obstructs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/benefit criteria for automated linen-loom engine
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics and claimed advantages used to evaluate the proposed engine that automates loom functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated evaluative measures: (1) one mill will set 10 or 12 looms to work (throughput); (2) the cloth may be made of what breadth you please or much broader than hitherto (capacity/flexibility); (3) fewer knots in the cloth because shuttle does not touch threads as much (quality/yarn integrity); (4) faster production and lower expense — fewer workmen required, one boy can tend multiple looms (labor efficiency/cost). These are the performance criteria emphasized when judging the machine's merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for anatomical post-mortem observation and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: What to observe and how to describe pathological findings during dissection to relate anatomy to clinical history. "The anatomy of morbid bodies ... is most instructive; thereby we become acquainted not only with the many causes that oppress nature, but with the liberty she often takes in forming the parts different from her usual rule."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record gross organ morphology (size, color, attachments), presence and character of suppuration (pus: quantity, fetor), cavities and sinuses, presence/number/size/colour/consistence/shape of calculi (stones), extent and anatomical distribution of lesions, unusual conformations (e.g. kidneys conjoined or dilated vena cava), vascular supply and anomalies (arteries/veins ramifications and insertion points), ureteral anatomy (number and course), and correlate these findings with the patient's symptoms and clinical course. Include figures/labels and measurements where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical observation and star-cataloguing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and methods used for compiling and correcting star catalogues and deriving astronomical parameters for navigational use. The author restored about 350 fixed stars omitted in Tycho's catalogue and produced tables for navigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sufficiently precise instruments and make assiduous observations even under poor skies; compare new observations with ancient catalogues (Clavius, Bartschius, Kepler) to reveal discrepancies; provide tables of right ascensions and distances from the pole for use by navigators; include appended observations (e.g. Mercury, lunar parallaxis attempts). For determining lunar parallaxis, propose geometric methods such as comparing meridian altitudes of the moon observed simultaneously at distant latitudes (e.g. St. Helena and Europe). Emphasize instrument description, recording of observational circumstances, and derivation of tables corrected to a reference year.
